---
title: "Does the President Set Gas Prices? 33 Years of Data Say No"
subtitle: "Gas follows crude oil. Each party has had cheap years and expensive years, with no pattern by party."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-09"
categories: [gas, politics, cost of living]
image: ../../images/cover.png
---

```{r setup}
# --- data -------------------------------------------------------------------
gas_dir <- "../../../gas_forecasting"   # the gas_forecasting project folder
source(file.path(gas_dir, "R", "gas_data_prep.R"))
library(plotly)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

dollars <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))

# inflation (CPI) from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
cpi <- read.csv("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=CPIAUCSL")
names(cpi) <- c("month", "cpi")
cpi$month <- as.Date(cpi$month)
latest_cpi_month <- max(cpi$month)
latest_cpi <- cpi$cpi[cpi$month == latest_cpi_month]

# weekly gas price in today's dollars
gas_weekly <- gas_weekly %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(date, "month")) %>%
  left_join(cpi, by = "month") %>%
  fill(cpi) %>%                                  # newest weeks use the latest CPI
  mutate(real_price = price * latest_cpi / cpi)

# Brent crude oil, monthly average ($/barrel)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), file.path(gas_dir, "database", "gas_data.db"))
crude <- dbGetQuery(con, "select period, price from crude_prices")
dbDisconnect(con)

crude_monthly <- crude %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(as.Date(period), "month")) %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(brent = mean(price), .groups = "drop")

gas_vs_oil <- gas_monthly %>% inner_join(crude_monthly, by = "month")
oil_fit    <- lm(price ~ brent, data = gas_vs_oil)
oil_r2     <- summary(oil_fit)$r.squared
cents_per_10_dollars <- coef(oil_fit)[["brent"]] * 10 * 100

# --- key numbers --------------------------------------------------------------
by_party <- gas_weekly %>%
  group_by(pres_party) %>%
  summarise(avg_real = mean(real_price), weeks = n(), .groups = "drop")

dem_avg <- by_party$avg_real[by_party$pres_party == "D"]
rep_avg <- by_party$avg_real[by_party$pres_party == "R"]

by_control <- gas_weekly %>%
  group_by(control) %>%
  summarise(avg_real = mean(real_price), .groups = "drop")

real_peak <- gas_weekly %>% slice_max(real_price, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
real_low  <- gas_weekly %>% slice_min(real_price, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
nominal_peak <- gas_weekly %>% slice_max(price, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
latest    <- gas_weekly %>% slice_max(date, n = 1)

real_label <- paste0(format(latest_cpi_month, "%B %Y"), " dollars")

first_week <- gas_weekly %>% slice_min(date, n = 1)   # example for explaining inflation

pres_avgs <- gas_weekly %>%                           # average per presidential term
  mutate(term_id = consecutive_id(president)) %>%
  group_by(term_id, president) %>%
  summarise(avg = mean(real_price), .groups = "drop")
```

Every time gas prices jump, someone blames the White House. Bumper stickers, memes, campaign ads: the
president gets the credit when prices fall and the blame when they rise.

So we checked. We lined up **every week of U.S. gas prices since April 1993**
(`r format(nrow(gas_weekly), big.mark = ",")` weeks, six presidential terms) against who held the
White House, the Senate, and the House.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Adjusted for inflation, the average gallon of gas cost `r dollars(dem_avg)` under Democratic presidents
and `r dollars(rep_avg)` under Republican presidents.**
:::

That tie looks suspicious, so to be clear: it's a coincidence of averaging. Individual presidencies range from
`r dollars(min(pres_avgs$avg))` a gallon (`r pres_avgs$president[which.min(pres_avgs$avg)]`) to
`r dollars(max(pres_avgs$avg))` (`r pres_avgs$president[which.max(pres_avgs$avg)]`), and both of those are Democrats.
Each party has had cheap years and expensive years. Leave out a single presidency and the party averages split
apart. What the tie *does* tell you is that there's no pattern by party.

**What "adjusted for inflation" means:** prices rise over time, so a dollar in 1993 bought more than a dollar
does now. To compare fairly, we convert every old price into today's money. For example, the
`r dollars(first_week$price)` a gallon drivers paid in `r year(first_week$date)` bought what
`r dollars(first_week$real_price)` buys today, so we count it as `r dollars(first_week$real_price)`.

What actually moves the price is crude oil, and crude oil answers to wars, OPEC, recessions, and
hurricanes, not to elections.

## 33 years of prices and who was in charge

Shading shows the president's party (**blue = Democrat, red = Republican**). Gold dots are major world
events. The strip underneath shows which party controlled the White House, Senate, and House.
Hover for details.

```{r timeline}
#| fig-height: 6.5
first_week <- min(gas_weekly$date)
last_week  <- max(gas_weekly$date)
top        <- max(gas_weekly$price) * 1.1

pres_bands <- presidencies %>%
  mutate(start = pmax(start, first_week), end = pmin(end, last_week),
         middle = start + (end - start) / 2)

events_on_chart <- key_events %>%
  left_join(gas_weekly %>% select(week = date, price), by = join_by(closest(date <= week))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(price))

price_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = pres_bands,
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = 0, ymax = top, fill = pres_party, text = label),
            alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_text(data = pres_bands, aes(x = middle, y = top * 0.96, label = president), size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = gas_weekly,
            aes(x = date, y = price, group = 1,
                text = paste0("Week of ", format(date, "%b %d, %Y"), "<br>", dollars(price),
                              "<br>President: ", president,
                              "<br>Senate: ", senate, " | House: ", house)),
            color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = events_on_chart,
             aes(x = week, y = price, text = paste0(event, "<br>", format(date, "%b %d, %Y"))),
             color = "#D69E2E", size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = party_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Price per gallon")

control_strip <- control_periods %>%
  filter(end > first_week) %>%
  mutate(start = pmax(start, first_week), end = pmin(end, last_week)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(pres_party, senate, house), names_to = "body", values_to = "party") %>%
  mutate(body = recode(body, pres_party = "White House", senate = "Senate", house = "House"),
         row  = match(body, c("House", "Senate", "White House")))

strip_plot <- ggplot(control_strip) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = row - 0.45, ymax = row + 0.45, fill = party,
                text = paste0(body, ": ", party, "<br>", format(start, "%b %Y"), " to ", format(end, "%b %Y"))),
            color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = party_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = c("House", "Senate", "White House")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "", y = "")

subplot(ggplotly(price_plot, tooltip = "text"),
        ggplotly(strip_plot, tooltip = "text"),
        nrows = 2, heights = c(0.78, 0.22), shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) %>%
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The chart above is in the dollars of each week, which makes recent years look worse than they were.
A dollar in 1993 bought a lot more than a dollar today, so for fair comparisons the rest of this post
uses **`r real_label`**.

## Finding 1: No pattern by party

```{r party chart}
#| fig-height: 3.5
party_compare <- bind_rows(
  by_party %>% transmute(group = ifelse(pres_party == "D", "Democratic president", "Republican president"),
                         avg_real, type = "White House"),
  by_control %>% transmute(group = case_when(control == "Unified D" ~ "Democrats control all three",
                                             control == "Unified R" ~ "Republicans control all three",
                                             TRUE ~ "Split control"),
                           avg_real, type = "All of Washington")
) %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = rev(group)))

party_plot <- ggplot(party_compare,
                     aes(x = avg_real, y = group,
                         text = paste0(group, ": ", dollars(avg_real), " per gallon"))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A9D8F", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = dollars(avg_real)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar, limits = c(0, 4.3)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = paste0("Average price per gallon, in ", real_label), x = "", y = "")

ggplotly(party_plot, tooltip = "text") %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

We see the same thing when we look at all of Washington. Republicans in full control, Democrats in full
control, or split government: the inflation-adjusted averages land within a few cents of each other. Same
caution as above: each group mixes cheap years with expensive ones, so the close numbers don't mean either
party lowers prices. They mean neither one has a track record of it.

## Finding 2: Crude oil is the steering wheel

Gasoline is made from crude oil, and crude oil is priced on a world market. Here's what gas prices would
have been if you predicted them **using nothing but the price of oil**, against what they actually were.

```{r oil chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
gas_vs_oil <- gas_vs_oil %>% mutate(oil_only = predict(oil_fit))

oil_plot <- ggplot(gas_vs_oil, aes(x = month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = price, color = "Actual gas price", group = 1,
                text = paste0(format(month, "%b %Y"), "<br>Actual: ", dollars(price))), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = oil_only, color = "Predicted from oil price alone", group = 1,
                text = paste0(format(month, "%b %Y"), "<br>Oil-only prediction: ", dollars(oil_only),
                              "<br>Brent crude: $", round(brent), "/barrel")),
            linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Actual gas price" = "grey20", "Predicted from oil price alone" = "#C05621")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Price per gallon", color = "")

ggplotly(oil_plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.1)) %>%
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The two lines barely separate. **The price of crude oil alone explains `r percent(oil_r2, accuracy = 1)` of the
ups and downs in monthly gas prices over 33 years.** As a rule of thumb, every \$10 change in a barrel of oil moves a
gallon of gas by about **`r round(cents_per_10_dollars)` cents**.

## Finding 3: Presidents can move oil, but they don't control it

Fair question: if oil drives gas prices, can't a president drive oil prices? **Sometimes, yes.** The
levers a president actually has:

- **Military action.** In 2026 the U.S. and Israel struck Iran, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was
  disrupted, and March 2026 saw the biggest one-month jump in gas prices in this data. That one traces
  straight back to a decision made in the White House.
- **Sanctions.** Limiting oil sales from countries like Iran, Venezuela, or Russia takes supply off the
  world market, which tends to push prices up.
- **The emergency oil reserve.** In 2022, the White House released 180 million barrels from the Strategic
  Petroleum Reserve, the largest release ever, to bring prices down.
- **Drilling and permits.** These matter, but new wells take years to come online, so the effect usually
  lands on a later president's watch.

But the biggest swings in this data came from things no president controlled:

- **2005:** Hurricane Katrina knocked out Gulf Coast refineries.
- **2008:** Oil hit nearly \$147 a barrel, then the financial crisis crushed demand. In today's dollars,
  the most expensive gas in this data was **`r format(real_peak$date, "%B %Y")`, at `r dollars(real_peak$real_price)` a gallon.**
- **2014–2015:** OPEC kept pumping into a glut and prices collapsed.
- **2020:** COVID lockdowns emptied the roads.
- **2022:** Russia invaded Ukraine, and the national average hit its all-time high of
  `r dollars(nominal_peak$price)` (`r format(nominal_peak$date, "%B %Y")`).

So a president's choices can push gas prices up or down, sometimes a lot. But presidents of both parties
have pulled these levers, and both have been on the receiving end of world events. Over 33 years it
evens out, with no party coming out ahead.

## Every presidency, side by side

```{r president table}
gas_weekly %>%
  mutate(term_id = consecutive_id(president)) %>%
  group_by(term_id, president, pres_party) %>%
  summarise(from = min(date), to = max(date),
            avg_real = mean(real_price),
            start_real = first(real_price), end_real = last(real_price),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  transmute(President = paste0(president, " (", pres_party, ")"),
            Years = paste0(year(from), "–", ifelse(to == max(to), "now", year(to))),
            `Average` = dollars(avg_real),
            `At start` = dollars(start_real),
            `At end`   = dollars(end_real),
            `Change`   = paste0(ifelse(end_real >= start_real, "+", "–"), dollars(abs(end_real - start_real)))) %>%
  kable(align = "llrrrr",
        caption = paste0("Average price per gallon, in ", real_label, ". Clinton's term starts in April 1993, when the weekly data begins."))
```

## The bottom line

Gas prices are a great way to feel the economy and a terrible way to grade a president. If you want to
know where prices are headed, watch the price of oil and the news from the Middle East, not the polls.

Right now the national average is **`r dollars(latest$price)`** (week of `r format(latest$date, "%B %d, %Y")`).
For where it's likely headed next, see our monthly gas price tracker.

---

**How we did this.** Weekly U.S. retail gasoline prices (all grades) and weekly Brent crude prices come
from the [U.S. Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/). Inflation
adjustments use the Consumer Price Index ([FRED, CPIAUCSL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL)),
converted to `r real_label`. Each week is assigned to whoever held the White House, Senate, and House
majority that day. The "oil only" line is a simple linear regression of the monthly gas price on the
monthly Brent price.
